name: Mazhar Jan-i Janan
bio: Mazhar of Delhi, of a family originally from Bokhara, is described in the book as learned in jurisprudence as well as poetry, with many favourite poets among his pupils, a Sunni who professed spiritual poverty and was reputed able to work miracles. The book says he was killed by a fanatic because he disagreed with the Shiah mourning for the death of Hussein, and died in 1780, aged nearly a hundred years.

The 5 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poems.title: No fault is thine, Beloved, I do not blame thee
poems.author: Mazhar Jan-i Janan
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
No fault is thine, Beloved, I do not blame thee,
Nor do I blame my rivals for their part,
I know my trouble causeless, yet I hearken
To my unreasonable, doubting heart.

poems.title: What thou hast done, never an enemy
poems.author: Mazhar Jan-i Janan
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
What thou hast done, never an enemy
Would practise on a bitterly-hated foe;
    And yet, my friend,
I took thee for a friend, and did not know.

poems.title: Mayhap my sorrowful heart
poems.author: Mazhar Jan-i Janan
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
Mayhap my sorrowful heart
Did not deserve thou shouldst bestow on me
Thy priceless love, but neither did it merit
    Thy cruel tyranny.

poems.title: She lightly laughed--And so is Mazhar dead?
poems.author: Mazhar Jan-i Janan
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
She lightly laughed--And so is Mazhar dead?
Alas, poor helpless one! I knew not I
What was his trouble.--Then again she said
--I did not think him ill enough to die.

poems.title: If I behold her, I am mad
poems.author: Mazhar Jan-i Janan
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
If I behold her, I am mad,
And if I see her not, I die;
O Love, to tender hearts like mine
Thou art a great calamity.
